question: A customer support agent handles a multi-issue session. After several turns the agent refers to "your recent refund request" instead of the specific $247.83 refund for order #8891. The conversation history is being summarised between turns. What is the most effective fix?
options: Increase the context window size so summarisation isn't needed at all
Extract transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers) into a persistent CASE FACTS BLOCK that is included in every prompt and never summarised
Instruct the model to "preserve all numerical values" during summarisation
Store the full conversation in an external database and retrieve relevant turns on demand
rationales: A larger window only delays the problem. Eventually it fills, and summarisation still destroys the specifics.

The progressive-summarisation trap systematically destroys numerical values and identifiers. The case facts block is the documented fix: critical facts live in their own structured block, included in every prompt, exempt from summarisation.
Prompt instructions to preserve specifics during summarisation are probabilistic and unreliable — the model still compresses details.
External retrieval adds infrastructure complexity without addressing the core requirement: which facts must persist in EVERY prompt.

question: A research synthesis agent combines output from three subagents into a final report. Critical findings from the SECOND subagent are consistently omitted, even though all three subagents produce high-quality outputs. Where should you look first?
options: The second subagent's prompt — perhaps it's not formatting outputs correctly
The synthesis agent's context window size — it may be running out of tokens
The POSITION of the second subagent's output in the aggregated input — "lost in the middle" may be burying it between the first and third agents' outputs
The synthesis agent's temperature setting — it may be too creative and ignoring details
rationales: The question states all three subagents produce high-quality outputs — formatting isn't the issue.
This isn't a capacity issue; it's a positional-attention issue.

The "lost in the middle" effect: long inputs are attended to most reliably at the beginning and end. Findings in the middle are systematically de-weighted. Mitigation: place a key findings summary at the start, then full content with clear headers.
Temperature controls randomness, not positional attention biases. This is unrelated.

question: An `order_lookup` tool returns 42 fields per result. The support agent only needs 5 fields to process a refund. After 8 turns, the agent's responses become slower and less accurate. What is the ROOT cause?
options: The model is hitting its maximum OUTPUT token limit
Untrimmed tool results accumulate in the conversation history; over 8 turns the irrelevant fields consume substantial input context
The order lookup tool is returning stale data after repeated calls
The model needs a higher temperature to maintain creativity in long conversations
rationales: Output token limits affect generation length, not comprehension across turns.

Each untrimmed 42-field result sits in conversation history forever. 8 turns × 42 fields ≈ 336 fields of accumulated noise (only ~40 of which were ever needed). Trim verbose tool outputs to relevant fields BEFORE they enter the context.
Staleness would cause incorrect data, not slower-and-less-accurate-everything.
Temperature is unrelated to context budget consumption.

question: A developer builds a multi-turn support agent. To save tokens, they include only the last 3 messages in each API request. Users report the agent "forgets" earlier context. Why?
options: The model's attention mechanism cannot handle conversations longer than 3 turns
The Claude API is STATELESS — each request must include the complete conversation history for coherence
The system prompt needs to instruct the model to remember earlier turns
The developer should use a different model with better long-term memory
rationales: The model can handle long conversations; the issue is that earlier messages are simply not being sent.
The API is stateless: there is no server-side session memory. Whatever you don't include in the request, the model doesn't see. Truncating to the last 3 messages literally removes earlier context.
The model cannot "remember" content it was never given. Prompt instructions can't recover messages omitted from the request.
All Claude API models are stateless. The fix is the truncation approach, not the model.

question: A multi-agent research pipeline has upstream research agents feeding findings to a downstream synthesis agent. The synthesis agent produces vague summaries without specific figures or citations. The research agents themselves produce detailed, accurate outputs. What should you change?
options: Give the synthesis agent a larger context window to accommodate all the research output
Reduce the number of upstream agents so the synthesis agent has less input to process
Modify upstream agents to return STRUCTURED DATA (key facts, citations, relevance scores) instead of verbose reasoning chains
Add a summarisation step between research and synthesis to compress the research output
rationales: More context space doesn't help when the input is buried verbose reasoning rather than structured facts.
Cutting agents reduces coverage. The problem is output format, not volume.
Upstream-agent optimisation: have research agents emit structured records (claim, source, date, relevance) so the downstream synthesis agent receives extractable signal instead of prose to re-parse.
Adding another summarisation step is exactly the wrong direction — it further destroys specific figures and citations.

question: What is the central failure mode that the "persistent case facts block" pattern is designed to prevent?
options: The model running out of context capacity during a long conversation
Progressive summarisation systematically destroying critical transactional details (amounts, dates, identifiers) as turns accumulate
Tool results returning malformed JSON
Two subagents producing contradictory output
rationales: Capacity exhaustion is a different problem; case facts blocks don't solve that directly.

Progressive summarisation is the documented anti-pattern: as a session is rolled up to save tokens, specific values are exactly the thing summaries discard. Case facts blocks exempt those values from summarisation.
Malformed JSON is a structured-output concern (Domain 4), unrelated to case-facts.
Contradictory subagent output is a multi-agent error-propagation concern, not what case-facts addresses.

question: Which technique most directly mitigates the "lost in the middle" effect in long inputs?
options: Increasing the temperature to encourage broader attention
Placing key findings or critical facts at the BEGINNING (and optionally END) of the input, with clear section headers and a brief summary at the top
Compressing the entire input into a single long paragraph for uniform processing
Asking the model to re-read the middle of the input before responding
rationales: Temperature changes randomness, not positional attention.

The documented mitigation is structural: put the most important content at positions the model attends to most reliably (start/end), use clear headers, and provide a summary at the top so middle content has anchoring context.
Removing structure makes the problem worse — clear section headers actually help.
"Re-read the middle" requests are unreliable and don't change the underlying positional bias.

question: A team's support agent calls a customer lookup tool that returns 40+ fields. After several turns, performance has degraded. Where SHOULD the trimming happen?
options: After the agent generates its response, removing fields the model didn't end up using
BEFORE the tool result enters the conversation history — e.g. in a PostToolUse hook or in the tool implementation itself, so only the needed fields are ever added to context
When the conversation reaches the model's context limit
Trimming isn't necessary; the model can ignore irrelevant fields
rationales: Post-response trimming has no effect on input tokens already spent.
The documented practice is to trim BEFORE the result enters context — at the tool layer or via a PostToolUse hook. Once verbose content is in the history, it costs tokens on every subsequent turn.
Waiting until the limit is hit means the cost has already been paid many times over.
Ignoring irrelevant fields still costs tokens. The model doesn't "skip" input it doesn't need; it processes everything it's given.

question: Which is the BEST description of an upstream agent's responsibility when feeding a downstream synthesis agent?
options: Provide the full transcript of the upstream agent's reasoning, so the downstream agent can audit how conclusions were reached
Provide STRUCTURED, EXTRACTABLE FINDINGS (claim + source + date + relevance), so the synthesis agent receives signal that doesn't need to be re-parsed and that fits its context budget
Provide a single-sentence summary only, to minimise context consumption
Provide the entire source documents the upstream agent consulted, for completeness
rationales: Verbose reasoning chains waste downstream context and bury the actual findings; this is the documented failure mode.
Upstream-agent optimisation: structured records with claim, source, date, and relevance score. The synthesis agent doesn't need to re-derive findings from reasoning — it composes them.
A single sentence is too compressed; you lose the specific facts and citations the synthesis report needs.
Forwarding source documents pushes the parsing burden downstream, which is exactly what good upstream-agent design avoids.

question: An engineer increases the model's context window from 200K to 1M tokens to "solve" intermittent context-degradation issues in a long-running agent. Three weeks later the same issues reappear. What's the most likely explanation?
options: Context-degradation issues like progressive summarisation, lost-in-the-middle, and untrimmed tool results are not solved by larger windows — they recur as soon as the larger window fills. The real fixes (case facts block, top-of-input summaries, tool-result trimming, structured upstream agents) are still needed
The new window isn't actually being used — a configuration issue
The model behaves worse with larger windows due to attention dilution
Context windows decrease over time as the model is updated
rationales: Larger windows postpone but don't solve the underlying structural problems: summarisation still destroys details, position bias still buries middle content, untrimmed tool results still accumulate, verbose upstream output still wastes budget. Real fixes are structural.
Configuration could be a one-off issue, but the pattern (worked, then degraded) is exactly the larger-window-fills-up story.
Attention dilution is a separate concern at the prompt-design level; the recurrence here is straightforwardly the larger window filling up.
Context windows don't decrease — and three weeks isn't a model-update cycle that would matter.

question: A support agent achieves only 55% first-contact resolution, well below the 80% target. Logs show it escalates straightforward damage-replacement cases while attempting to autonomously handle complex policy-exception requests. What is the most effective improvement?
options: Implement sentiment analysis to detect customer frustration and automatically escalate when negative sentiment exceeds a threshold
Have the agent self-report a confidence score (1–10) and automatically route to humans when confidence falls below a threshold
Add EXPLICIT ESCALATION CRITERIA to the system prompt with FEW-SHOT EXAMPLES demonstrating when to escalate versus resolve autonomously
Deploy a separate classifier model trained on historical tickets to predict escalation
rationales: Sentiment is uncorrelated with case complexity. This would escalate frustrated-but-straightforward cases and miss calm-but-complex ones.
LLM self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated. The agent is already mis-confident on hard cases and uncertain on easy ones; routing on its own confidence won't fix this.
Explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples directly address the unclear decision boundary. This is the proportionate first step before adding ML infrastructure.
Over-engineered — labelled data + classifier infrastructure when prompt optimisation hasn't been tried.

question: A customer writes: "This is absolutely ridiculous! My package arrived completely smashed. I paid good money for this." The damage-replacement policy clearly covers this case. What should the agent do?
options: Escalate to a human agent because the customer is clearly frustrated
Acknowledge the frustration, apologise, and offer to process the damage replacement immediately
Ask the customer if they would prefer to speak with a human before proceeding
Report a low confidence score and route to human review
rationales: Frustration does not trigger escalation. The issue is covered by policy; the agent should resolve it.
The frustration nuance: when the issue is resolvable, ACKNOWLEDGE the emotion and OFFER the resolution. Don't escalate a straightforward case just because the customer is upset.
Pre-emptively offering a human on a straightforward case wastes human capacity and delays resolution. The agent should just resolve it.
Self-reported confidence is unreliable. Don't route on it.

question: A customer's FIRST message is: "I want to speak to a real person, not a chatbot." What should the agent do?
options: Acknowledge the request but first attempt to resolve the issue, since it might be simple
Ask the customer what their issue is so the human has context for the handoff
ESCALATE TO A HUMAN AGENT IMMEDIATELY without any investigation or attempt to resolve
Explain the agent's capabilities and offer to help before escalating
rationales: An explicit human request must be honoured immediately. No "let me try first" — that's the anti-pattern.
Gathering context first still violates the immediate-escalation rule. The human agent can gather context themselves.
Explicit human request → immediate escalation. No exceptions, no delays.
Trying to convince the customer to use the agent contradicts the absolute rule.

question: A customer asks to return a product purchased from a COMPETITOR at your store. Your return policy is silent on competitor purchases. What is this situation, and what should happen?
options: A policy violation — the policy doesn't allow competitor returns, so deny the request
A POLICY GAP — the policy is silent, so this requires human judgement to decide whether to make an exception; escalate
A straightforward case — apply the standard return policy regardless of where it was purchased
An ambiguous case — ask the customer to clarify what they want
rationales: Violation means the policy explicitly says no. Silence ≠ violation.
Policy gap: policy doesn't address this. The agent cannot make the exception unilaterally; escalate for human judgement. Gaps require escalation; violations have documented answers.
Applying the standard return policy to a competitor product may violate business rules. The policy doesn't authorise the agent to decide.
The customer's request is clear; the ambiguity is in the policy, not the request.

question: A customer lookup by name returns three records for "Sarah Johnson" — one active last week, one three months ago, one last year. What should the agent do?
options: Select the most recently active record as the most likely caller
Select the record matching the caller's area code or location, if available
ASK THE CUSTOMER for an additional identifier such as email address, phone number, or order number
Present all three records and ask the customer to confirm which is theirs
rationales: Heuristic selection on recency risks acting on the wrong account — privacy violation and potentially incorrect financial action.
Location-based heuristics are equally unreliable and can produce wrong-account actions.
The only safe approach is to request a disambiguating identifier from the customer. Never pick by heuristic when multiple records match.
Displaying all three records leaks personal data of the other customers to the caller — a serious privacy violation.

question: Which is NOT a valid escalation trigger?
options: The customer explicitly requests a human
The request falls outside documented policy (a policy gap requiring human judgement)
The agent has attempted resolution and cannot make meaningful progress
The agent's self-reported confidence is below a fixed threshold
rationales: Explicit human request — a valid trigger, requiring immediate escalation.
Policy gap — a valid trigger.
Genuine inability to progress after good-faith resolution attempts — a valid trigger.
Self-reported LLM confidence is poorly calibrated and unreliable as a routing signal. It's not a valid escalation trigger.

question: A customer asks: "What is your store's return window?" — straightforward, fully documented. The agent picks up on "slight irritation" in the message and routes to a human. What's wrong with this decision?
options: Frustration / sentiment is not a valid escalation trigger; routing a fully-resolvable, documented question to a human wastes human capacity and degrades response time
The agent should have escalated sooner, before the irritation grew
The agent should have asked for more information first
Nothing — when in doubt, always escalate
rationales: Sentiment-driven escalation on resolvable cases is the documented anti-pattern: it doesn't correlate with complexity, and it floods the human queue with cases the agent should have handled.
There's no reason to escalate at all — the question is fully answerable from policy.
More information isn't needed; the question is concrete and clear.
"When in doubt, escalate" is exactly the heuristic that produced the 55%-resolution problem.

question: A customer says, "I'm so frustrated, my order is late." The agent looks up the order, confirms it's late, and offers a documented goodwill credit + reshipment. The customer says, "No, I want to talk to a human." What should the agent do?
options: Try again to resolve, because they didn't request a human in the first message
Argue that the offered resolution is generous and should be sufficient
Escalate immediately — the customer has now explicitly requested a human, which is an absolute escalation trigger regardless of when in the conversation it arrives
Lower the agent's confidence score and let the routing system decide
rationales: Explicit human request is absolute — it doesn't have to be the first message.
Arguing against a customer's explicit human request is the wrong response and damages trust.
Once the customer explicitly asks for a human, escalate. The earlier resolution attempt was correct; the explicit request now overrides further autonomous handling.
Confidence-based routing isn't the mechanism for explicit human requests — those are immediate escalations.

question: Which is the RIGHT relationship between escalation triggers and self-reported confidence?
options: Confidence is the primary trigger; explicit human request and policy gap are secondary signals
Confidence is one of several signals weighted together, with explicit human request weighted highest
Explicit human request, policy gap, and inability to progress are the primary triggers; uncalibrated self-reported confidence is NOT a valid escalation signal on its own
Confidence and explicit human request are equivalent and interchangeable triggers
rationales: Confidence is not a primary trigger; it's an unreliable signal that doesn't appear in the documented trigger list.
Weighted combination still relies on confidence; the documented rule is that confidence is not a valid trigger because it isn't calibrated.
The three documented triggers are explicit human request, policy gap, and genuine inability to progress. LLM self-confidence is not on the list because it isn't calibrated.
They're not equivalent — explicit human request is absolute; confidence is unreliable.

question: A team replaces sentiment-based and confidence-based escalation with explicit escalation criteria + few-shot examples in the system prompt. First-contact resolution rises from 55% to 78%. Why was this so effective?
options: Few-shot examples train the model to be more confident on hard cases

Explicit criteria + examples gave the agent an unambiguous decision boundary aligned with policy, and removed two unreliable signals (sentiment, self-confidence) that were causing miscategorisation in both directions
Removing escalation altogether forced the agent to attempt everything
The temperature change improved consistency
rationales: Few-shot examples don't change the model's confidence; they change its decision boundary.

The lift came from (a) replacing vague "use your judgement" with explicit criteria and concrete examples, AND (b) removing two unreliable signals (sentiment / self-confidence) that were driving misclassification in opposite directions.
Escalation wasn't removed — it was redirected to the actual valid triggers.
Temperature wasn't changed; this is about criteria, not sampling settings.

question: A web-search subagent in a multi-agent research system times out while researching a topic. You need to design how this failure information flows back to the coordinator. Which approach best enables intelligent recovery?
options: Return STRUCTURED ERROR CONTEXT including failure type, attempted query, partial results, and potential alternative approaches
Implement automatic retry with exponential backoff, then return a generic "search unavailable" status only after all retries are exhausted
Catch the timeout and return an empty result set marked as successful
Propagate the timeout exception to a top-level handler that terminates the entire research workflow
rationales: Structured error context (type, what was tried, partials, alternatives) gives the coordinator everything it needs to choose recovery: retry, alternative source, partial-results synthesis, or human escalation.
A generic "unavailable" status hides the query, partial results, and alternatives. Even after retries fail, the coordinator can't make an informed recovery decision.
Silent suppression — the WORST anti-pattern. The coordinator believes the search succeeded and found nothing, so it never tries alternatives and produces an invisible gap.
Workflow termination wastes successful partial results from the OTHER subagents.

question: A subagent searches a database for customer orders and returns zero results. The subagent's code catches all exceptions and returns `{results: [], status: "success"}`. The database was actually experiencing intermittent connectivity issues. What is this failure pattern called?
options: Graceful degradation
SILENT SUPPRESSION
Workflow termination
Defensive programming
rationales: Graceful degradation reduces functionality while acknowledging the limitation. This hides the failure entirely — opposite.
Silent suppression: a failure is masked as a success, so the coordinator (and the report) treats "no results" as the real answer. The documented worst anti-pattern in multi-agent error propagation.
Workflow termination would crash the pipeline. Silent suppression keeps running but with invisible gaps.
Defensive programming would propagate structured error context, not mask failures.

question: A research pipeline has 5 subagents. Subagent 3 fails with a timeout. The system terminates the entire pipeline. What is the primary COST of this approach?
options: The timeout will not be logged for debugging
The user receives an unhelpful error message
Partial results from the 4 subagents that completed successfully are thrown away
The failed subagent cannot be restarted independently
rationales: Logging is a separate concern, orthogonal to termination policy.
Error-message wording is a UX concern; not the principal cost.

Workflow termination is the second documented anti-pattern: it discards work the other agents completed successfully. The right approach is selective propagation that lets the coordinator continue with partials.
Independent restart is a benefit of structured error propagation, not a cost of termination per se.

question: A subagent searches an academic database and returns zero results. Should the coordinator retry this search?
options: Yes, always retry zero-result searches in case of intermittent connectivity
It depends — if the search EXECUTED SUCCESSFULLY and found no matches, no retry is needed. If the search FAILED TO CONNECT, retry is warranted
No, zero results means the data does not exist and retrying wastes time
Yes, but only with modified search parameters to broaden the query
rationales: Retrying a successful query that genuinely found nothing wastes time on a query that will always return nothing.

The critical distinction: ACCESS FAILURE (couldn't reach source — retry warranted) vs VALID EMPTY RESULT (reached source, no matches — that IS the answer). The coordinator needs structured error context to know which is which.
Zero results from a failed connection is NOT the same as zero results from a successful query. You must distinguish them.
Broadening the query is appropriate for some access-failure scenarios, but if the original query executed and genuinely found nothing, broadening is a separate decision.

question: A synthesis agent combines findings from three research subagents. One subagent failed to retrieve journal articles on geothermal energy. The synthesis report covers solar and wind thoroughly but does not mention geothermal. What is the correct approach?
options: The report is acceptable — if the data wasn't available, the topic should simply be excluded
Add a COVERAGE ANNOTATION noting that the geothermal section is limited due to unavailable journal access
Delay the report until the geothermal research can be completed
Estimate geothermal findings based on the solar and wind data as a reasonable proxy
rationales: Silently omitting the topic makes the gap invisible. A reader would assume geothermal wasn't relevant, not that the source was unavailable.

Coverage annotations explicitly note which areas have gaps and why. Transparency lets the consumer know what the report covers fully and where there are known limitations — without silent suppression and without halting the whole pipeline.
Delaying the entire report for one failed section is the workflow-termination anti-pattern in another dress.
Fabricating findings via proxy is exactly what NOT to do — provenance integrity matters more than apparent completeness.

question: Which fields are MOST important for a subagent to include when returning a structured error to the coordinator?
options: Just `status: error` and a human-readable message
Failure type (e.g. access / validation / permission / no-data), what was attempted (query, parameters), any partial results, and recommended next steps or alternatives
The full exception stack trace from the underlying SDK
A self-reported confidence score on the error itself
rationales: Status + message is too little; the coordinator can't decide between retry, alternative, partial synthesis, or escalation.
These are the documented elements of structured error context. They enable INTELLIGENT recovery rather than blunt all-or-nothing reactions.
Stack traces are useful for debugging but not actionable for the coordinator's recovery decision.
Self-reported confidence on the error doesn't add useful information; the failure type is what drives recovery.

question: An access failure occurs in a customer-lookup subagent. The coordinator retries 3 times with exponential backoff; all retries fail. What should happen NEXT?
options: Continue retrying indefinitely
Mark the workflow as failed and abort everything

Return a structured error to the user-facing layer with the failure type, what was attempted, and alternatives (e.g. "try again later" or "contact support"), plus any partial results gathered before the failure
Silently return an empty result and continue
rationales: Unbounded retry burns resources and breaks SLAs.
Aborting everything discards any partial work from other agents and provides no useful information to the user.
After retries exhaust, propagate structured error context upward. The next layer (or user) can make an informed decision based on failure type + alternatives.
Silent suppression — the documented worst anti-pattern.

question: A coordinator receives a structured error from a subagent containing partial results from 3 of 5 sources. The other 2 sources timed out. What is the correct downstream behaviour for the SYNTHESIS step?
options: Discard the partials and synthesise nothing, since the data is incomplete
Synthesise on the partials and clearly annotate which sources are missing and why, so the final report's gaps are visible to the consumer
Wait until all sources can be re-fetched before synthesising
Fabricate findings for the missing 2 sources to keep the report uniform
rationales: Discarding partial results that succeeded wastes successful work — the workflow-termination anti-pattern.
Synthesise on what you have AND annotate the gaps. Coverage annotations are the documented mechanism for honest, partial-data reporting.
Waiting indefinitely is a denial-of-service in disguise.
Fabrication destroys provenance and is far worse than transparent gaps.

question: What is the principal difference between SILENT SUPPRESSION and a VALID EMPTY RESULT?
options: Silent suppression returns no data; valid empty result returns metadata
Silent suppression MASKS a failure (the operation actually failed but is reported as success); valid empty result REPORTS HONESTLY that an operation succeeded and found nothing matching the query
Silent suppression is intentional; valid empty result is accidental
Silent suppression is acceptable in some cases; valid empty results are always bugs
rationales: Both can return no data; the difference is whether the underlying status is truthful.

Silent suppression: real failure presented as success — coordinator can't recover. Valid empty result: real success with no matches — coordinator should accept and move on. The status field must be truthful.
Silent suppression is rarely "intentional" in a defensible sense — it's usually a poorly-designed catch-all. Both states can be deliberate.
Valid empty results are useful, honest signals. Silent suppression is the anti-pattern.

question: Which design choice MOST helps a coordinator distinguish access failures from valid empty results?
options: Always retry zero-result responses several times before accepting them

Include both a structured status field (e.g. `success` / `access_error` / `permission_denied` / `no_match`) AND, where applicable, a brief description of what was attempted and any partial results — so the coordinator can branch correctly without retries
Use exception throwing universally and let the coordinator catch them
Embed the difference in the natural-language response and let the LLM coordinator parse it
rationales: Always retrying conflates the two cases (success-with-no-match becomes indistinguishable from access failure).

Distinct status values + attempted-action context + partials let the coordinator branch its recovery deterministically: retry for access errors, accept for `no_match`, escalate for permission issues, and so on.
Exception throwing alone doesn't carry the semantics (was it an access error or no data?) the coordinator needs.
LLM-parsing of natural language is exactly the kind of probabilistic, fragile design that structured error propagation is meant to replace.

question: A developer productivity agent is exploring an unfamiliar codebase. After investigating several modules, it starts referencing "typical repository patterns" instead of the specific class names and dependency chains it discovered earlier. What is the most effective mitigation?
options: Increase the model's context window to accommodate more discovery output
Have the agent maintain SCRATCHPAD FILES recording key findings, and reference them for subsequent questions
Restart the session and ask the agent to explore more efficiently
Pre-load the entire codebase structure into the initial context before exploration begins
rationales: Context degradation isn't a capacity problem — a bigger window just delays it. The model still loses grip on earlier findings as verbose output accumulates.

Scratchpad files persist knowledge OUTSIDE the conversation context. The agent records specific findings (class names, dependency chains, decisions) and reads them back as needed. Mitigates degradation directly.
Restarting loses accumulated knowledge and doesn't address the underlying problem — degradation will recur in the new session.
Pre-loading consumes context budget before exploration even starts AND doesn't help with degradation during the session.

question: A codebase exploration agent delegates investigation to three subagents. The main agent's context stays clean while subagents handle verbose file reading and search operations. What is the PRIMARY benefit?
options: Parallelisation — the three subagents investigate simultaneously, reducing wall-clock time
Cost reduction — subagents use cheaper model tiers for routine file reading
CONTEXT ISOLATION — the main agent's context is not filled with verbose exploration output
Error handling — subagent failures do not crash the main agent
rationales: Parallelisation is a secondary benefit; the primary value for codebase exploration is keeping the main agent's context clean.
Model-tier selection is a separate concern; delegation for context isolation is independent of which model each agent uses.
Subagent delegation for exploration is primarily about context isolation. The main agent retains high-level coordination context; subagents absorb the verbose output in their own isolated contexts.
Error handling is enabled by structured error propagation, not by delegation per se.

question: An agent completes Phase 1 of codebase exploration (architecture overview) and is about to spawn subagents for Phase 2 (detailed component investigation). What should happen between phases?
options: The subagents should start fresh and re-discover the architecture to verify Phase 1 findings
Phase 1 findings should be SUMMARISED AND INJECTED into the Phase 2 subagent prompts
The full Phase 1 verbose output should be passed directly to Phase 2 subagents for complete context
Phase 2 subagents should read the Phase 1 conversation log from storage
rationales: Re-discovery duplicates work and wastes Phase 2 context budget on already-known information.

Summary injection: distil Phase 1 findings into a concise summary and inject it into Phase 2 prompts. Phase 2 agents start with the architectural context they need WITHOUT the verbose discovery noise.
Passing verbose output defeats the purpose of context isolation — Phase 2 agents would start with contexts already cluttered with Phase 1 exploration.
Full conversation logs include verbose discovery output. Summaries are the correct transfer mechanism.

question: During an extended codebase exploration session in Claude Code, the agent's context is filling with verbose file contents and search results. When should the `/compact` command be used?
options: Only when the agent hits the context limit and can no longer process new input
PROACTIVELY during the session to maintain context quality before limits are reached
At the end of the session to create a clean summary for the next session
Only when the agent explicitly reports that it is losing track of earlier findings
rationales: Waiting until the hard limit means quality has already been degrading for some time.
`/compact` is a tool for maintaining context QUALITY proactively, not just capacity. Use it during extended sessions before degradation sets in.
End-of-session compaction misses the chance to maintain quality throughout the session.
By the time the agent reports losing track, outputs have already been affected. Proactive use prevents this.

question: A codebase exploration session crashes after 45 minutes of investigation. The agent had discovered critical dependency chains and test-coverage gaps. Without any recovery mechanism, what happens?
options: The model retains findings from the session and can continue in a new session
All exploration progress is lost and must be repeated from scratch
The findings are preserved in the model's long-term memory for future sessions
The conversation history is automatically saved and can be resumed
rationales: The Claude API is stateless. There's no session memory persisting across separate API calls or sessions.

Without explicit state persistence (scratchpad files, structured state manifests at checkpoints), all progress is lost on crash. This is why long-running exploration agents should checkpoint state to files.
LLMs have no long-term memory across sessions. Each session starts fresh unless state is explicitly persisted.
Conversation history is not automatically saved for API-based usage. The developer must implement persistence.

question: What is CONTEXT DEGRADATION, distinct from running out of context capacity?
options: A drop in model quality as the context approaches its hard token limit

A loss of grip on earlier findings as verbose discovery output accumulates — the model starts speaking in generalities ("typical patterns") instead of citing the specific classes / dependencies it had previously identified
Model drift from being retrained on the conversation
A network slowdown affecting API responses
rationales: Hard-limit issues are a related but distinct problem.

Context degradation is when the model loses sharpness on specifics it discovered earlier, because verbose accumulated output crowds out and dilutes the salient findings. The symptom is generalities replacing specifics. Mitigations: scratchpad files, subagent isolation, proactive `/compact`.
Models aren't retrained during a session.
Network slowdowns aren't a model behaviour, just an operational issue.

question: An agent is investigating a 500-file codebase. It reads files A, B, C, D, then 50 more, and is now asked to recall the dependency chain involving A. The agent gives a vague answer about "typical patterns" instead of the specifics it found in A. What's the BEST structural mitigation?
options: Re-read file A and hope the new read overrides the degraded memory

When findings about A were originally established, record them in a scratchpad file. Read that scratchpad file back when the question about A arises — the durable record is outside the conversation context and is unaffected by the intervening 50 files
Increase temperature to encourage more specific output
Ask the question in a way that triggers reasoning rather than recall
rationales: Re-reading the file works for a single file but doesn't scale — and the re-read joins the same noisy context.

Scratchpad files are the documented structural mitigation. Specific findings persist outside the conversation. When the agent needs to refer back, it reads the scratchpad, not its degraded conversation memory.
Temperature changes randomness, not specificity recall.
Reasoning over verbose accumulated context produces the same degradation — that's what created the problem.

question: Which is the strongest argument AGAINST simply pre-loading the entire codebase into the initial context to "avoid degradation"?
options: Pre-loading is technically not allowed by the API

Pre-loading consumes a large portion of the context budget upfront — leaving less for actual exploration and reasoning — and it doesn't prevent degradation when verbose discovery output accumulates over the session anyway
The model can only process one file at a time
Pre-loading triggers higher rate limits
rationales: There's no API rule against it; the objection is design, not policy.

Pre-loading is the worst of both worlds: you pay the full token cost upfront, and you still get degradation as exploration output accumulates. Scratchpad files, subagent isolation, and proactive `/compact` are the right mitigations.
The model can process many files; that's not the constraint.
Token volume affects cost, not rate-limit thresholds directly.

question: Why do SUBAGENTS help with codebase-exploration context degradation specifically?
options: Subagents process information faster than the main agent
Each subagent has its own isolated context, so the main agent doesn't accumulate verbose file reads and search results — it only sees the structured findings each subagent returns
Subagents share memory with the main agent so findings transfer automatically
Subagents bypass the model's attention mechanism
rationales: Speed isn't the differentiating factor for degradation.

Each subagent has its own context. They absorb the verbose stuff and return only the structured findings. The main agent sees only the digested output, preserving its context budget and avoiding the degradation that comes from verbose accumulation.
Subagents do not share memory; that's exactly why this design works.
Subagents use the same attention mechanism as any model invocation.

question: Which combination is the recommended multi-pronged approach to managing context in a long codebase-exploration session?
options: Just use scratchpad files
Just use the `/compact` command at the end
Combine scratchpad files (persistent findings), subagent delegation (context isolation), proactive `/compact` use, and structured state manifests at checkpoints for crash recovery
Increase the context window and disable all other techniques
rationales: Scratchpad files alone help, but don't isolate exploration noise from the main context.
End-of-session compaction misses the chance to maintain quality during the session.

All four work together: scratchpads (durable findings outside conversation), subagents (context isolation), proactive `/compact` (quality maintenance during the session), and state manifests (crash recovery). No single technique covers all four failure modes.
Larger windows postpone problems but don't solve them; disabling the actual mitigations makes things worse.

question: A structured data extraction system achieves 97% overall accuracy across all document types. The team proposes automating all extractions where model confidence exceeds 95% to reduce human review costs. What is the critical RISK?
options: The 95% confidence threshold is too low and should be raised to 99% for automation
Aggregate accuracy may MASK POOR PERFORMANCE on specific document types or fields, and confidence scores need CALIBRATION against labelled validation sets before use
The model will become overconfident over time as it processes more documents, requiring regular retraining
Automated extractions should always have human review regardless of confidence, making the proposal fundamentally flawed
rationales: Threshold value isn't the core issue. Aggregate metrics hide per-type disparities regardless of where the threshold is set.

97% overall can hide 40% error rates on specific document types. Without stratified validation by document type / field AND calibration of confidence scores against labelled data, automation will silently fail on certain inputs.
LLMs don't train during inference. The issue is existing calibration gaps across document types, not model drift.
Automation is valid when properly validated per type / field. The issue is making the decision based on UNCALIBRATED aggregate metrics.

question: A team implements a review system that routes all extractions with model confidence below 0.80 to human reviewers. Extractions above 0.80 are fully automated. What is MISSING from this approach?
options: The 0.80 threshold is too low and should be raised to 0.95
STRATIFIED RANDOM SAMPLING of high-confidence automated extractions to detect novel error patterns
A second model to verify the first model's extractions before automation
Human review of all extractions regardless of confidence for the first month
rationales: Raising the threshold doesn't address the blind spot. Any novel error pattern in high-confidence items still goes undetected.

Low-confidence items already get reviewed. The blind spot is the HIGH-confidence automated stream — if a novel error pattern emerges there, no one sees it. Stratified random sampling of automated extractions catches this.
A second model adds cost without addressing the fundamental need for ongoing human verification of automated outputs.
A one-month review period is a one-off check, not the ongoing detection mechanism stratified sampling provides.

question: A model reports 0.92 confidence on a date extraction from a STANDARD INVOICE and 0.92 confidence on a date extraction from a HANDWRITTEN RECEIPT. Should these be treated the same way?
options: Yes, the same confidence score indicates the same reliability regardless of document type
No — raw confidence scores are not calibrated. 0.92 on invoices may correspond to 98% actual accuracy while 0.92 on receipts may correspond to only 70%. Apply per-document-type calibration
Yes, but only if both document types were included in the training data
No, handwritten receipts should always go to human review regardless of confidence
rationales: Raw model confidence is not calibrated. The same score means different things across different document-field combinations.

Confidence scores must be calibrated using labelled validation sets PER document type / field. The calibration curve will likely show that 0.92 on invoices is far more reliable than 0.92 on handwritten receipts.
Inclusion in training data doesn't guarantee calibrated confidence. Calibration against ground truth is always required.
While handwritten receipts may often need more review, the correct mechanism is calibrated thresholds per type — not blanket rules.

question: A review team has 5 reviewers handling 500 extractions per day. Currently, items are assigned in chronological order. How should the queue be restructured?
options: Assign items randomly to ensure fair distribution across document types
Assign items by document type so each reviewer specialises
Order the queue by UNCERTAINTY so each reviewer always gets the highest-uncertainty item remaining
Divide items equally among reviewers to balance workload
rationales: Random assignment still wastes reviewer time on high-confidence items.
Specialisation may help, but it doesn't address WHICH items most need a human.

Prioritise by uncertainty: limited human capacity should be applied where it adds the most value — at the highest-uncertainty items. When a reviewer finishes one item, the next should be the highest-uncertainty item remaining.
Equal division is essentially chronological with extra steps — same wasted capacity on high-confidence items.

question: What is the correct SEQUENCE for reducing human review on automated extractions?
options: Measure aggregate accuracy → Set a confidence threshold → Automate above threshold → Sample occasionally
Measure accuracy by document type and field → Calibrate confidence with labelled data → Set calibrated thresholds → Implement stratified sampling → Reduce review on VALIDATED segments only
Run the system for 30 days → Calculate error rate → Automate if error rate is acceptable
Start with full automation → Add human review only for fields that show errors in production
rationales: Uses aggregate accuracy (the trap) and uncalibrated thresholds. Occasional sampling is insufficient.

Each step prevents a specific failure: per-type measurement prevents the aggregate trap, calibration prevents unreliable thresholds, stratified sampling provides ongoing verification, and only validated segments get reduced review.
30-day aggregate is the same trap on a larger scale; novel errors can emerge later.
Starting with full automation before validation guarantees undetected errors. Review precedes automation, not the reverse.

question: What is the principal purpose of STRATIFIED RANDOM SAMPLING of automated extractions in a review system?
options: To audit reviewer performance
To detect novel error patterns in the high-confidence automated stream that would otherwise be invisible — providing ongoing verification that calibration assumptions still hold
To balance reviewer workload
To reduce model latency
rationales: Reviewer auditing is a separate concern.

High-confidence items don't get reviewed in normal flow. Stratified sampling provides ongoing verification that the calibration assumption still holds, catching novel error patterns before they cause downstream damage.
Workload balancing is a queue concern, not the sampling purpose.
Sampling doesn't change model latency.

question: What is the correct relationship between AGGREGATE accuracy and PER-FIELD accuracy when deciding to automate extractions?
options: Aggregate accuracy is the more important signal because it represents the overall system
Per-field (and per-document-type) accuracy is critical — aggregate can hide severe weakness in specific fields or document types, making automation decisions based on aggregate dangerous
They are interchangeable
Aggregate accuracy is only relevant for batch metrics; per-field accuracy is for individual extractions
rationales: Aggregate is exactly the trap. 97% aggregate can hide 40% per-field failure on certain fields or types.

Per-field and per-document-type accuracy reveal where the model genuinely performs reliably and where it doesn't. Automation decisions need to be made at this granularity to avoid silent failure modes.
They are not interchangeable — aggregate can mask the per-field disparities that matter for safe automation.
Per-field accuracy is fundamental for automation decisions; aggregate is too coarse.

question: A team observes that the model's self-reported confidence is 0.91 on a class of inputs where actual accuracy (from labelled data) is only 74%. What does this tell us?
options: The model is broken and should be replaced

Raw confidence is poorly calibrated in this range / for this input class; for routing decisions, replace raw confidence with a calibrated threshold derived from the labelled data (e.g. "route to review when raw confidence < 0.95" if 0.95 raw corresponds to acceptable actual accuracy)
Confidence should not be reported at all
The labelled data is wrong
rationales: Poor calibration is a known property of raw LLM confidence, not a sign of brokenness.
Use the labelled data to derive the calibrated mapping. Routing thresholds should be based on actual accuracy, not raw confidence. "0.91 raw" means different things in different input classes.
Confidence can still be useful — once calibrated. The signal isn't worthless; it just needs translation.
Labelled data, properly collected, is the ground truth that exposes the calibration gap. Don't blame ground truth for revealing the gap.

question: A team currently spends substantial reviewer time on high-confidence automated extractions "just in case". A leader proposes eliminating those reviews entirely. What's the better design?
options: Eliminate them entirely — they're a sunk cost on already-validated items

Replace blanket review of all high-confidence items with STRATIFIED RANDOM SAMPLING of that automated stream, plus per-field / per-document-type accuracy monitoring; this catches novel error patterns without paying the full review cost
Double down on full review for high-confidence items to be safe
Reroute the budget to lower the threshold and review more items below 0.80
rationales: Eliminating ongoing verification entirely leaves you blind to novel error patterns. Cost reduction is fine; abandoning observability isn't.
Stratified sampling provides ongoing verification at a fraction of the cost. Combined with per-field accuracy monitoring, it detects novel error patterns before they cause downstream damage.
Doubling down is wasteful and doesn't address the issue being raised.
Lowering the threshold to review more items adds review cost on items that probably don't need it; it doesn't address the high-confidence blind spot.

question: Which is true about LLM SELF-REPORTED CONFIDENCE as a routing signal?
options: It is highly reliable and should be used directly to make automation decisions
It is poorly calibrated by default, especially across heterogeneous input types, and must be CALIBRATED AGAINST LABELLED DATA before being used to drive automation or routing decisions
It is irrelevant — only model size predicts accuracy
It only matters for tool use, not extraction
rationales: Raw confidence is the documented unreliable signal. Direct use leads to silent failures.
Calibration against labelled data is required to translate raw confidence into actionable thresholds. Without it, confidence numbers can be confidently wrong on certain input classes.
Confidence isn't irrelevant — it just needs calibration to be useful.
Confidence calibration matters across many use cases, including extraction and code review, not just tool use.

question: A multi-agent research system produces a synthesis report on market trends. Two credible sources report different growth rates: Source A reports 12% growth (2023 data) and Source B reports 8% growth (2024 data). The synthesis agent currently selects the more recent value. What is the correct approach?
options: Always use the most recent source as it reflects the latest data
Average the two values and report 10% growth with a note about source variance
Annotate both values with source attribution and publication dates, letting the consumer decide how to interpret the difference
Flag the conflict and escalate to a human researcher for resolution before including in the report
rationales: Silently discarding the older value destroys valid historical context. The difference may reflect a real trend (growth deceleration), not a data-quality issue.
Averaging conflicting statistics is mathematically misleading and destroys the temporal context that explains the difference.
Preserve provenance, temporal context, and both data points. The consumer can see that different dates explain different numbers and interpret accordingly. This is the documented provenance practice.
Unnecessary escalation — the values aren't truly contradictory when temporal context is considered. Proper annotation with dates resolves the apparent conflict.

question: A synthesis agent combines findings from three research subagents. The final report states: "renewable energy investment has grown significantly" without citing any specific source or figure. What went wrong?
options: The research subagents did not find specific figures
The synthesis agent paraphrased findings without preserving CLAIM-SOURCE MAPPINGS
The report is appropriately summarised for executive readability
The synthesis agent correctly abstracted away unnecessary detail
rationales: The question implies subagents produced detailed findings. The failure is at the synthesis step.

Attribution dies during summarisation when the synthesis agent compresses findings without preserving claim-source mappings. The original likely read "$495 billion in 2023 (IEA World Energy Report 2024)" — flattened to "has grown significantly."
Removing specific figures and sources isn't summarisation — it's information destruction. Executive summaries should still cite sources and key figures.
Dropping attribution and figures isn't abstraction — it's loss of provenance. The synthesis agent must explicitly preserve claim-source mappings.

question: A multi-agent research pipeline has four steps: (1) research subagent collects findings, (2) analysis subagent evaluates findings, (3) synthesis subagent combines findings, (4) report generation. At which step is attribution MOST commonly lost?
options: Step 1 — research subagents often fail to record sources
Step 2 — analysis subagents strip source information during evaluation
Step 3 — synthesis subagents combine and paraphrase without carrying source mappings forward
Step 4 — report generation formats remove inline citations
rationales: With structured claim-source mappings, sources are captured at collection. Proper schema design addresses this step.
Analysis subagents typically ADD evaluation onto findings; they don't usually strip sources unless misdesigned.

Synthesis is the documented most-common failure point. The agent naturally compresses and paraphrases; without explicit instructions to preserve claim-source mappings, attribution disappears during the merge.
Report generation is mechanical formatting. If citations exist in the synthesis output, they'll be formatted into the report.

question: A synthesis report needs to present three types of content: quarterly investment figures by sector, a narrative about regulatory changes, and a list of API integration patterns. How should these be rendered?
options: All as prose paragraphs for consistent formatting throughout the report
All as structured tables for easy scanning and comparison
Investment figures as tables, regulatory narrative as prose, API patterns as structured lists
All as bullet-pointed lists for maximum readability
rationales: Forcing financial data into prose makes it harder to compare values. Forcing technical patterns into prose obscures structure.
Narrative regulatory changes read unnaturally as tables. Tables are for comparing values, not storytelling.
Content-appropriate rendering: financial data as tables (numbers + comparisons), narrative as prose (cause-and-effect, chronology), technical findings as structured lists (specifications, patterns).
Bullet lists work for technical findings but are wrong for financial comparisons (need tables) and narrative context (need prose).

question: An analysis agent encounters two documents reporting different annual revenue figures for the same company: $4.2M from the annual report and $3.8M from an SEC filing. What should the analysis agent do?
options: Use the annual report figure as it is more authoritative
Flag the conflict and stop analysis until a human resolves it
Complete the analysis with both values annotated, including source context and a possible explanation for the difference (e.g. audited vs preliminary, fiscal vs calendar year)
Average the two figures and report $4.0M as the estimated revenue
rationales: Arbitrarily selecting one value destroys information. Both come from legitimate sources with different reporting bases (audited vs preliminary; fiscal vs calendar). Both are valid.
Stopping analysis is disproportionate; the conflict can be annotated and analysis completed. The coordinator or consumer decides how to handle it.

Complete the analysis with conflicts intact and explicitly annotated. Include both values, their sources, and a possible explanation. The decision on how to handle the conflict belongs to the coordinator or consumer.
Averaging conflicting figures is mathematically misleading and destroys the source context that explains the difference.

question: Which of the following is the BEST design pattern for preserving provenance through a synthesis pipeline?
options: Trust each agent to remember its own sources
Use STRUCTURED CLAIM-SOURCE MAPPINGS (e.g. `{claim, source, date, confidence}`) that subagents produce, analysis agents extend, and synthesis agents must preserve and merge
Add inline citations only at the report-generation step
Rely on the LLM to infer sources from context at synthesis time
rationales: "Trust to remember" is the documented failure mode at the synthesis step.
Structured claim-source mappings make provenance a first-class data structure that passes through the pipeline. Each layer preserves and extends it; nothing summarises it away.
Adding citations only at report generation is too late — by then the synthesis has already lost the mappings.
Inferring sources at synthesis time is exactly what produces "has grown significantly" outputs.

question: A reader of a synthesis report should be able to do which of the following?
options: Trust every claim is correct without verification
Trace each claim back to the source it came from, including publication date, so they can verify and assess relevance themselves
See only the synthesis agent's interpretation, not the underlying sources
Assume the synthesis agent has reconciled all conflicts in the most accurate way
rationales: Synthesis output should be verifiable, not faith-based.
Traceability is a core deliverable. Claim → source → date → context is the minimum provenance package; the reader can verify and assess relevance themselves.
Hiding sources is the failure mode that produces unverifiable, unciteable reports.
Reconciliation choices should be transparent and annotated, not hidden behind opaque interpretation.

question: Which of the following is NOT an appropriate response to conflicting sources in a synthesis report?
options: Annotate both sources with publication dates and let the reader interpret the difference
Annotate both sources with a possible explanation (e.g. fiscal vs calendar year, audited vs preliminary)
Silently choose the more recent source and report only that value
Where one source is clearly outdated and another supersedes it, document the supersession explicitly while still naming both sources
rationales: Appropriate: temporal annotation lets the reader interpret apparent disagreement as a possible trend.
Appropriate: domain context explains structural reasons for the difference.
INAPPROPRIATE — silent selection destroys provenance and may mislead the reader. The other three options preserve information transparently.
Appropriate when supersession is genuinely the case; both sources are still named so the reader can verify.

question: A synthesis report's authority depends on TRACEABILITY. Which combination MOST damages traceability?
options: Paraphrasing claims, dropping source attributions, and stating bare conclusions without dates
Quoting verbatim from each source with full attribution
Using structured tables for numbers and prose for narrative
Annotating conflicts with publication dates and possible explanations
rationales: This is the documented failure mode: paraphrase + dropped attribution + missing dates = unverifiable claims. Each loss compounds.
Verbatim quotation with attribution is the strongest form of traceability.
Content-appropriate rendering improves readability without harming traceability.
Annotating conflicts with context strengthens traceability rather than damaging it.

question: A synthesis report needs to handle a case where ONE source is from 2020 and ANOTHER source is from 2024. The 2020 source reports 15% market share for Vendor X; the 2024 source reports 22%. What is the BEST treatment?
options: Report only the 2024 figure
Report only the 2020 figure
Report both figures with their respective publication years, framing the difference as a trend (Vendor X's share grew from 15% in 2020 to 22% in 2024 per <Source A, 2020> and <Source B, 2024>)
Average them to 18.5%
rationales: Reporting only the newer value discards the trend context that gives the newer figure meaning.
Reporting only the older value is also wrong — the situation has changed.

Both values are valid AT THEIR RESPECTIVE DATES. Framing them as a trend with both sources cited preserves provenance and surfaces the real story (growth). This is the documented practice for temporally-separated, both-valid sources.
Averaging 2020 and 2024 produces a number that represents nothing real. The dates matter.
